concepts.text: Fundamental Rights: General Nature and Features
children: Guaranteed to all persons without discrimination
Aim at equality, dignity, individual liberty, and larger public interest
Protect against authoritarian and despotic rule
Establish government of laws and not of men
Promote political democracy and unity of the nation
Available only to citizens for some rights (e.g., Articles 15,16,19,30) and to all persons for others (e.g., 14,20,21)
Not absolute; subject to reasonable restrictions determined by courts
Balance individual rights with social control and public interest
Some FRs are negative (limitations on State), some positive (conferring privileges)
Justiciable; enforceable directly by Supreme Court under Article 32
Ordinary law cannot curtail FRs; they can be amended only by constitutional amendment subject to basic structure
Can be suspended during National Emergency, except Articles 20 and 21
Most FRs are self-executory; a few require parliamentary legislation
Uniformity throughout the country (Article 35)
Bedrock of democratic system
Formidable bulwark of individual liberty
Establishment of rule of law
Protection of minorities and weaker sections
Strengthen secular fabric of Indian State
Check on absolutism of government authority
Foundation of social equality and social justice
Ensure dignity and respect of individuals
Facilitate participation in political and administrative process
Excessive limitations: numerous exceptions, restrictions, qualifications
No social and economic rights (right to work, social security, etc.)
Vague and ambiguous terms (public order, minority, reasonable restriction)
Expensive remedy; common man cannot afford
Rights benefit mainly rich section of society
Preventive detention (Article 22) negates individual liberty
Suspension during emergency cuts at roots of democracy
No consistent philosophy (Sir Ivor Jennings)
Government and Parliament of India (executive and legislative of Union)
Government and legislatures of states (executive and legislative of state)
Local authorities (municipalities, panchayats, district boards, improvement trusts)
Other authorities (statutory or non-statutory like LIC, ONGC, SAIL)
Private body or agency acting as instrument of State (Supreme Court interpretation)

concepts.text: Article 13: Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
children: Doctrine of judicial review: power of Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) to declare laws void if inconsistent with FRs
Definition of law includes permanent laws, temporary laws (ordinances), statutory instruments (order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification), and custom or usage having force of law
Constitutional amendments are not law under Article 13 (Kesavananda Bharati case)
Constitutional amendment can be challenged if it violates basic structure

concepts.text: Article 14: Equality before Law and Equal Protection of Laws
children: Equality before law (British concept): absence of special privileges, equal subjection to ordinary law, no person above law
Equal protection of laws (American concept): equality under equal circumstances, like treated alike
Equality before law is negative; equal protection is positive
Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia and substantial distinction
Rule of Law as embodied in Article 14 is a basic feature of the Constitution
Exceptions to equality rule: immunities of President/Governor (Article 361), foreign sovereigns and diplomats, Article 31-C laws giving effect to Directive Principles
Applies to both citizens and foreigners
Prohibits discrimination by State on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth (first provision)
Also prohibits discrimination by private individuals in access to public places (shops, restaurants, wells, roads, etc.) (second provision)
Exceptions: special provisions for women and children (a)
Exceptions: special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs, STs (b)
Special provision for admission to educational institutions for backward classes (c) – added by 93rd Amendment (2005)
Special provision for economically weaker sections (EWS) – added by 103rd Amendment (2019), 10% reservation in educational institutions
Reservation for OBCs in central educational institutions: 27% quota upheld by Supreme Court subject to creamy layer exclusion
EWS eligibility criteria: family gross annual income below ₹8 lakh and exclusion based on land/property holdings

concepts.text: Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment
children: No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence
Parliament can prescribe residence condition for certain employment (expired 1974, except for Andhra and Telangana under Article 371D)
State can provide reservation for backward class not adequately represented (Article 16(4))
Law can require incumbent of religious office to belong to that religion
State can provide reservation up to 10% for economically weaker sections (103rd Amendment, 2019)
Mandal Commission (1979): identified 3743 castes as OBCs, recommended 27% reservation; implemented in 1990
Indra Sawhney case (1992): upheld 27% reservation with conditions: creamy layer exclusion, 50% ceiling, no reservation in promotions (later modified)

77th Amendment (1995) allowed reservation in promotions; 85th Amendment (2001) provided consequential seniority; 81st Amendment (2000) addressed backlog vacancies; 76th Amendment (1994) placed Tamil Nadu 69% reservation in Ninth Schedule
EWS reservation in public employment: 10% quota for persons not covered by existing reservations, eligibility based on family income and assets
Enforcement of disability arising out of untouchability is an offence punishable by law
Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955, renamed Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 (1976)
Untouchability not defined; refers to social disabilities based on birth in certain castes
Right under Article 17 is available against private individuals; State has constitutional obligation to ensure compliance
State cannot confer any title except military or academic distinction
Citizen cannot accept any title from foreign state
Foreigner holding office of profit under State cannot accept title from foreign state without President's consent
Hereditary titles (Maharaja, Raj Bahadur, etc.) banned
National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma awards) are not titles; cannot be used as suffixes or prefixes; instituted in 1954, discontinued 1977-1980, revived
Right to freedom of speech and expression
Right to assemble peaceably and without arms
Right to form associations or unions or co-operative societies
Right to move freely throughout the territory of India
Right to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India
Right to practice any profession or carry on any occupation, trade, or business
Originally seven rights; right to property deleted by 44th Amendment (1978)
These rights protected only against State action, not private individuals; available only to citizens (including shareholders of a company)
Reasonable restrictions on grounds mentioned: sovereignty and integrity of India, security of State, etc.
Freedom of speech includes press, advertisements, telecast, right to know, freedom of silence, etc.
Freedom of assembly: peaceful and unarmed; Section 144 CrPC and unlawful assembly (Section 141 IPC) restrict violent assemblies
Freedom of association: includes political parties, trade unions; no right to strike or effective bargaining guaranteed
Freedom of movement: covers internal movement only; external movement under Article 21
Freedom of residence: covers temporary stay and permanent domicile; restrictions for tribal areas and public health
Freedom of profession: State can prescribe qualifications; can carry on business exclusively or in competition; immoral or dangerous activities can be prohibited

concepts.text: Article 20: Protection in respect of Conviction for Offences
children: No ex-post-facto law: no conviction for violation of law in force at time of commission; no penalty greater than that prescribed at time of commission
No double jeopardy: no person prosecuted and punished for same offence more than once
No self-incrimination: no accused compelled to be a witness against himself
Ex-post-facto protection only for criminal laws, not civil or tax laws; also does not prevent trial under a later procedure
Double jeopardy applies only to proceedings before court of law or judicial tribunal, not departmental or administrative proceedings
Self-incrimination extends to oral and documentary evidence, but not to compulsory production of material objects, thumb impression, specimen signature, blood samples, or exhibition of body

concepts.text: Article 21: Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
children: Available to both citizens and non-citizens
Gopalan case (1950): narrow interpretation – protection only against arbitrary executive action, not legislative; 'procedure established by law' unlike 'due process'
Menaka case (1978): overruled Gopalan – procedure must be reasonable, fair, and just; introduced due process; protects against arbitrary legislative action
Right to life includes right to live with human dignity, not mere animal existence

Personal liberty of widest amplitude; includes many rights declared post-Menaka: right to livelihood, privacy, shelter, health, free education up to 14 years, free legal aid, speedy trial, travel abroad, and many more
Right against solitary confinement, handcuffing, inhuman treatment, delayed execution, custodial harassment, bonded labour, public hanging, noise pollution, etc.
Enforcement through Article 32 or Article 226
Free and compulsory education to children aged six to fourteen years
Added by 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002
Earlier non-enforceable Directive Principle under Article 45; Article 45 now deals with early childhood care
Supreme Court (1993) recognised primary education as fundamental right under Article 21
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009: full-time elementary education in formal school with norms and standards

concepts.text: Article 22: Protection against Arrest and Detention
children: First part (ordinary law): rights of arrested person – to be informed of grounds, to consult and be defended by legal practitioner, to be produced before magistrate within 24 hours, to be released after 24 hours unless magistrate authorises detention
These safeguards not available to enemy alien or persons detained under preventive detention law
Applies to criminal or quasi-criminal acts; does not cover civil arrest, arrest by court order, etc.
Second part (preventive detention): detention cannot exceed three months unless advisory board of High Court judges reports sufficient cause
Grounds of detention must be communicated to detenu; facts against public interest need not be disclosed; detenu has right to make representation
Parliament can prescribe classes of offences for detention beyond three months without advisory board
Legislative power: Parliament exclusive for defence, foreign affairs, security of India; concurrent for security of state, public order, supplies
Various preventive detention laws: Preventive Detention Act 1950 (expired), MISA, COFEPOSA, NASA, TADA, POTA, UAPA, etc.
No democratic country except India has made preventive detention an integral part of its Constitution

Article 23: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour – includes selling/buying of persons, immoral traffic, beggar (forced labour without remuneration), bonded labour; exception for State compulsory service for public purposes without pay, but without discrimination on religion, race, caste, class

Article 24: Prohibition of employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, and hazardous activities; harmless or innocent work not prohibited; Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 and related laws; Supreme Court directed Child Labour Rehabilitation Welfare Fund

Article 25: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion – subject to public order, morality, health; State can regulate secular activities and provide for social reform; wearing of kirpans included; Hindus include Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists

Article 26: Freedom to manage religious affairs – rights of religious denominations to establish institutions, manage own affairs, own property, administer property subject to law; conditions for denomination: system of beliefs, common organisation, distinctive name
Article 27: Freedom from taxation for promotion of any particular religion – State cannot compel taxes for support of any religion; fee for pilgrims or regulation of endowments is permissible

Article 28: Freedom from attending religious instruction or worship in certain institutions – no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions (exception for endowments requiring it); in recognised/aided institutions, voluntary with consent; four types of educational institutions distinguished

Article 29: Protection of interests of minorities – right of any section with distinct language, script, culture to conserve it; no denial of admission to State-maintained or aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste, language

Article 30: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions – applies to religious and linguistic minorities; includes right to choose governing body, appoint staff, admit students, set fee structure; three types: seeking aid+recognition, only recognition, neither; subject to regulatory measures for standards but not maladministration; aid does not dilute right; compensation for compulsory acquisition
Dr. Ambedkar called it the very soul and heart of the Constitution; a basic feature
Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
Supreme Court can issue directions, orders, and writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto
Concurrent jurisdiction with High Courts under Article 226
Alternative remedy is not a bar to relief under Article 32
Right cannot be suspended except during National Emergency under Article 359

concepts.text: Writs for Enforcement of Fundamental Rights
children: Habeas corpus: order to produce detainee before court to examine legality; bulwark of individual liberty; issuable against public authorities and private individuals; not issued if detention lawful
Mandamus: command to public official to perform mandatory duty; not against private individuals or President/Governor; not for discretionary duties
Prohibition: to forbid lower court/tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction; only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities; preventive
Certiorari: to quash order of lower court/tribunal or administrative authority affecting rights; both preventive and curative; not against legislative bodies
Quo-warranto: to inquire into legality of claim to a public office; prevents illegal usurpation; can be sought by any interested person

Article 31A: Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc. – five categories of laws saved from challenge under Articles 14 and 19; requires President's assent; compensation at market value for land under personal cultivation

Article 31B: Validation of acts and regulations in Ninth Schedule – originally blanket immunity from FR challenge; I.R. Coelho case (2007) limited immunity to laws before April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date); later laws open to challenge if they violate Articles 14,15,19,21 or basic structure

Article 31C: Saving of laws giving effect to Directive Principles under Article 39(b) or (c) – inserted by 25th Amendment; provision allowing declaration as conclusive struck down in Kesavananda; 42nd Amendment extended to all DPs but struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)

concepts.text: Restrictions for Armed Forces and Martial Law (Articles 33-34)
children: Article 33: Parliament can restrict/abrogate FRs for members of armed forces, paramilitary, police, intelligence agencies to ensure proper discharge of duties and discipline; laws not challengeable; examples: Army Act, Navy Act, Air Force Act, Police Forces Act, etc.

Article 34: Restrictions during martial law – Parliament can indemnify acts done for restoration of order and validate sentences; martial law means military rule, implicit in Constitution; different from National Emergency; does not automatically suspend habeas corpus

concepts.text: Right to Property: From Fundamental Right to Legal Right
children: Originally a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31
Most controversial FR; led to several constitutional amendments (1st, 4th, 7th, 25th, 39th, 40th, 42nd)
Abolished as Fundamental Right by 44th Amendment Act, 1978; became a legal right under Article 300A in Part XII

Now not part of basic structure; protected only against executive action, not legislative; cannot move Supreme Court directly under Article 32; no guaranteed compensation except for minority institutions (Article 30) and land under personal cultivation (Article 31A)
Established in Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)
Constitutional amendments can be challenged if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution
Basic structure includes judicial review, rule of law, federalism, secularism, democracy, etc.
Limits Parliament's power to amend the Constitution

concepts.text: Suspension of Fundamental Rights during National Emergency
children: President can suspend enforcement of FRs (except Articles 20 and 21) under Article 359 during National Emergency
Article 19 can be suspended only on grounds of war or external aggression, not internal armed rebellion
Suspension is by order; duration during emergency
Articles 20 and 21 are never suspendable
